sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Let's explore how Java treats primitive types like objects! Wrapper classes are your new best friends when you need to work with primitives in an object-oriented way.

• What wrapper classes are and why they exist
• How to convert between primitives and objects automatically
• Practical uses of wrapper classes in real code

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
sections.content:
Imagine you're at a party where everyone speaks different languages. Primitives (like `int`, `double`) speak 'basic data', while objects speak 'fancy Java'. Wrapper classes are like translators that help them communicate!

Java provides wrapper classes for all primitive types:
• `Integer` for `int`
• `Double` for `double`
• `Boolean` for `boolean`
• And more for all other primitives

These classes 'wrap' the primitive value in an object, giving you superpowers like:
• Storing numbers in ArrayLists (which only hold objects)
• Using methods to convert between types
• Handling null values safely

sections.title: 📊 Visual Simulation
sections.content: Step-by-step visualization of how Wrapper Classes work:

steps.title: Primitive to Wrapper
steps.description: Java automatically converts a primitive to its wrapper class when needed (called autoboxing)
steps.code:
int num = 42;
Integer wrappedNum = num; // Autoboxing happens here!

steps.title: Wrapper to Primitive
steps.description: Java also converts back automatically when you need the primitive value (called unboxing)
steps.code:
Integer wrappedNum = 42;
int num = wrappedNum; // Unboxing happens here!

steps.title: Using Wrapper Methods
steps.description: Wrapper classes provide useful methods like converting strings to numbers
steps.code:
String numberStr = "123";
int num = Integer.parseInt(numberStr); // Converts string to int

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ Wrapper classes turn primitives into objects (e.g., `int` → `Integer`)
✓ Autoboxing converts primitives to wrappers automatically
✓ Unboxing converts wrappers back to primitives automatically
✓ Wrapper classes provide useful methods like `parseInt()`
✓ All wrapper classes are immutable (can't change their value)

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Use wrapper classes when you need to store primitives in collections
Take advantage of wrapper methods like `valueOf()` and `parseXxx()`
Remember that wrapper objects can be `null` (unlike primitives)
donts: Don't compare wrapper objects with `==` (use `.equals()` instead)
Don't create unnecessary wrapper objects (let autoboxing handle it)
Don't forget that wrapper classes are immutable
sections.protip: Use `Integer.valueOf()` instead of `new Integer()` - it's more memory efficient because it caches common values!

sections.title: 🌍 Real World Use
sections.content: Where are wrapper classes used in real apps?

examples.how: When reading numbers from a database, they often come as wrapper objects (like `Integer`) because database fields can be null
ArrayLists and HashMaps can only store objects, so you need wrapper classes to store numbers (e.g., `ArrayList<Integer>`)
When reading settings from files, you often parse strings into numbers using wrapper methods like `Integer.parseInt()`

problem.description: Write a method that takes an ArrayList of Integer objects and returns the sum of all even numbers. Handle null values safely (treat them as 0).
hints: Use a for-each loop to iterate through the list
Check for null values before unboxing
Use the modulus operator (%) to check for even numbers
problem.explanation: We iterate through each Integer in the list. We first check if it's not null, then check if it's even using the modulus operator. If both conditions are true, we add it to our sum.

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 Wrapper classes bridge the gap between primitives and objects
📌 Autoboxing and unboxing make conversions automatic and painless
📌 Always handle null values when working with wrapper objects
📌 Practice using wrapper methods like `parseInt()` and `valueOf()`
📌 You're now ready to use primitives in object-oriented contexts!
